references.text: Joseph's interpretation of Pharaoh's dream predicts seven years of severe famine that would consume the land – the same famine now described in Gen 47:13.
The famine begins in all lands, and everyone comes to Egypt to buy grain from Joseph – the direct background for the situation in Gen 47:13.
The psalmist describes how God called forth famine over the land and broke every staff of bread – a poetic summary of the same famine that struck Egypt and Canaan.
The direct continuation describing the consequences of the famine: the people first give their money, then their livestock, and finally their land and themselves to Pharaoh.
Abraham also went down to Egypt because of famine in the land – a pattern repeated in the patriarchal narratives.
The severe famine in the land forces Jacob to send his sons back to Egypt to buy more grain.
Stephen's summary in the New Testament confirms and reaffirms the specific geographical and historical context from Joseph's time in the Old Testament.
These verses mark respectively the beginning and end of the seven-year famine, showing how Egypt's preparations were eventually exhausted.
The verses show the progression from having stored supplies to total lack, emphasizing the extremity of the famine.
The verses link the global influx with the local depletion of resources in Egypt.
The verse establishes the reason for the family's arrival in Egypt, which led to the situation where both Canaan and Egypt were without bread.
